opening_message:
Ticket 1: Diana Cooper (employee ID E020) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E020.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Engineer (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: admin
  - comment: Diana Cooper (E020) is a full-time Engineer. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, so admin is permitted.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Engineer (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB lists Diana Cooper (E020) as a contractor with basic security training, conflicting with HR note claiming full-time. As a contractor with basic training, maximum access is read; admin is not permitted. Recommend read for Source Code.
reason: The HR note claims Diana Cooper is a full-time Engineer (which would permit admin on Source Code), but the Security note, based on its database lookup, states she is a contractor with basic security training, for whom admin is never permitted and the maximum is read. Given the conflicting employment-type evidence and that contractor status categorically excludes admin, I apply the more restrictive, secure interpretation: the requested admin level exceeds the maximum allowable level, so I grant the maximum of read.

Access policy:

2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

If full_time Engineer: Source Code owned by Engineer role, so admin permitted -> grant admin (requested level is admin, at max).
If contractor with basic training: max is read -> grant read.
